#10452. AI is making software easier to build. Keeping it running is another story

These days, it almost feels like old news: Developers can now use AI tools to generate code, build features, and make changes in a fraction of the time they once needed. The problem now surfacing across businesses is that once software goes into production, teams still need to monitor, maintain, and fix it. A feature that takes minutes to build can introduce problems that take engineers hours to investigate.

Google’s 2025 DORA report, based on responses from nearly 5,000 technology professionals, found that greater AI adoption was associated with faster software delivery but reduced stability. While the researchers didn’t establish that AI-generated code directly caused more outages, their findings suggest that companies can produce software faster without necessarily becoming better at maintaining it.

That raises a critical question for companies investing heavily in AI coding tools: If development keeps getting faster, how much of the work involved in running software can also be automated? A growing group of companies is working to find out, developing AI systems that can investigate failures, identify possible causes, and, in some cases, take corrective action without waiting for an engineer.

MORE SOFTWARE, MORE TO MANAGE

Ishay Yaari, cofounder and CEO of DataAgent, a company developing autonomous remediation software, says the operational side of software development hasn’t advanced at the same pace as coding.

“More code, more frequent deployments, and more infrastructure changes naturally create more potential failure points,” he tells Fast Company.

For site reliability engineering (SRE) teams, that means managing applications and infrastructure that may be changing more frequently. When something fails, engineers must figure out what changed, identify the cause, and restore service.

Consider an application that begins crashing after an update. The cause could be faulty code, an incorrect configuration, insufficient computing resources, or a problem with another service. While monitoring tools may detect the failure immediately, engineers still need to examine logs, review recent changes, and investigate several possibilities before deciding what to fix.

Yaari says companies often respond to growing complexity by adding monitoring tools and collecting more data. That can help engineers see what’s happening, but it can also mean more alerts to investigate without necessarily improving how quickly problems are resolved.

The pressure isn’t necessarily coming from poor-quality AI-generated code. Even reliable code can be difficult to manage when applications, infrastructure, and dependencies are changing frequently.

In a recent analysis of AI-assisted development, Google’s DORA researchers found that developers saved time generating code but spent more time reviewing and verifying it. They also emphasized the importance of testing, feedback, and established engineering practices in turning faster development into better results.

For companies, that means the benefits of AI coding tools may depend partly on what happens after developers finish writing the code, particularly the ability of SRE teams to keep applications running reliably.

GIVING AI THE KEYS TO PRODUCTION

Software monitoring and observability tools have traditionally helped engineers detect problems and understand their causes. Now companies are trying to automate more of the response.

DataAgent is pursuing that approach. Its platform is designed to monitor applications and cloud infrastructure, identify potential issues, and help investigate them. Yaari wants AI to take on more of the operational work engineers currently perform manually.

Some failures have familiar remedies. An application might repeatedly crash because it doesn’t have enough memory. A deployment might fail because of an incorrect configuration. Or a new release might introduce errors that disappear when the system returns to an earlier version.

Companies already use automation to address certain problems through predefined rules. AI could extend that capability by examining the circumstances, identifying likely causes, and selecting an appropriate response.

Yaari says DataAgent’s platform is designed to understand both the infrastructure supporting an application and the application itself, including how services interact, what the application is expected to do, and how its behavior changes after an update.

The aim is to recognize problems that don’t fit a predefined rule. But identifying a likely solution is one thing. Allowing software to make changes to a live application is another.

Consider a deployment that introduces errors. Rolling back to the previous version may restore service, but if the update also changed a database or introduced new dependencies, reversing it could create additional problems. That’s why the ability to act matters as much as the ability to diagnose.

HOW MUCH SHOULD AI BE ALLOWED TO FIX?

In its 2026 State of AI-First Operations report, PagerDuty found that 44% of surveyed organizations required human involvement when AI was used to fix problems affecting customer-facing systems, while 43% required it when coordinating incident responses across teams.

Even companies adopting AI for operational work appear reluctant to give it unrestricted authority over critical systems.

Yaari agrees that some decisions should remain with people. He points to actions such as deleting large amounts of data, disabling security controls, or exposing sensitive information as examples that should require approval.

“The goal is not to remove humans from SRE; it is to remove humans from the repetitive operational work that machines can handle safely,” he says.

Companies must determine which systems an AI agent can access, what changes it can make, and when it must request approval. They also need records of what the agent did, particularly when an attempted fix fails.

Another consideration is the cost of monitoring and observability software. Applications generate vast amounts of logs, performance measurements, and other operational data. Companies pay to collect, store, and analyze that information, often across several platforms. Adding AI can create further expenses if it requires transferring large amounts of data to external services.

Yaari argues that more analysis should happen closer to where applications run. DataAgent is pursuing a distributed approach, with agents deployed within customers’ infrastructure to reduce the amount of data sent elsewhere.

Its published documentation describes local monitoring alongside cloud-based AI analysis and guided incident investigation. Yaari’s responses describe broader autonomous remediation capabilities. The company has not provided independent performance data establishing how much operational work or cost those capabilities can eliminate.

WHAT HAPPENS TO THE ENGINEER?

Yaari expects engineers to spend less time investigating repetitive incidents and more time designing systems, setting operational policies, and deciding what automated tools should be allowed to do.

“The fundamental shift is from people operating infrastructure to people managing autonomous infrastructure,” he says.

That could allow smaller engineering teams to support more applications, but it would also require them to understand how automated systems make decisions—and what happens when those decisions are wrong.

Engineering skills may evolve as a result. System architecture, security, reliability, and the ability to investigate unusual failures could become more important as routine operational work becomes easier to automate.

Google’s DORA research found that organizations with strong engineering practices were better positioned to benefit from AI-assisted development. The same lesson may apply to AI-powered operations. Companies will still need reliable processes for testing changes, responding to incidents, and evaluating whether automated fixes work.

The software industry has made considerable progress in helping developers produce code faster. Now it’s trying to bring some of that speed to keeping applications running.

If AI eventually handles both, engineers may spend less time performing individual tasks and more time deciding what the systems they build should do, how they should behave, and when a person needs to intervene.

#10450. Thinking of quitting your job? Don’t until you consider this factor

You know that stinging sensation you get when your coworker gets the promotion that you thought was yours? Or that sinking feeling of doom when you realize that a new hire could take over your role? Most likely, that voice within will tell you: “You’re falling behind.”

You are, however, likely ignoring an important emotional experience happening at the same time. It’s envy: simply wanting something that someone else has. Because of the stigma and shame attached to this “deadly sin,” we tend to want to suppress envy without even knowing it. It’s understandable, but also a huge inadvertent mistake.

If you’re a conscientious high achiever, or someone smart and caring, it is easy to see someone else’s success and start questioning your situation. Envy is a universal emotion. It is also normal to wonder if it’s time to make a big change, like looking for a new job or even a new career. But examining your envy first can help you avoid costly career pitfalls.

Beware of ‘Premature Game Switching’

A common reaction to workplace envy that I see among my coaching clients is to make a change. This feels like being proactive, but it is giving up on the current situation too soon, or what I call “premature game switching.” You see someone getting ahead or getting what you want in the game you’re playing. You jump the gun and assess that you can’t obtain what you want or win at this game, so you opt out and choose a different contest.

Doing something feels better than doing nothing. When we avoid taking a beat to study our envy, however, we ignore critical data.

All negative emotions have what is called “signaling value,” demanding that we pay attention to what is important. Fear helps us see danger. Grief occurs when we lose someone dear. Envy helps us see what we truly desire and avoid “desire confusion.”

Thanks to savvy advertisers and social media, we are inundated with opportunities to feel what the philosopher and critic René Girard called “mimetic desire.” We tend to want things that those around us want. While “keeping up with the Joneses” used to include only neighbors or people we encounter in real life, the blast radius for envy has widened. Now we can see many more things that many more people have. We don’t often see how these cloud our judgment.

Envy gives us a chance to see what we really want.

Heed the SIReN

To examine envy, start by looking at its four key components, or “SIReN.”

First, S is “similar target.” According to the social psychologist Abraham Tesser’s Self-Evaluation Maintenance model, we tend to compare ourselves to those who are just ahead of us, our peers or our coworkers. We envy them, while we admire those far beyond us. This provides hope, telling us that we’re not as behind as we think we are. You feel envious of the promotion, for example, because it was within your reach.

Second, I is “intangible desire.” What we truly want is not the thing itself but the feelings we believe we will experience once we have it. It isn’t really the promotion, but what it represents to you, which could be a variety of things: financial security, recognition as an expert, or the opportunity to mentor others.

Third, Re stands for “relevant comparison.” We envy in domains or areas that are important to us. If we care about our careers, we’re likely to experience career envy. It pinpoints more specifically what matters to us and where we may want to focus more energy. I, for example, don’t envy people who have podcasts, but I do envy other nonfiction authors.

Finally, N is “negative emotion.” The unpleasant feeling is a gauge. If we’re able to close the app and forget about what we saw, the envy was fleeting and perhaps not worth dwelling on. If it lingers long after you put down your smartphone, you may want to take another look at why you’re feeling that way.

Next, Channel Envy in the Right Direction

Social scientists, including Jens Lange and Jan Crusius, have shown there are two kinds of envy: benign and malicious. Malicious envy tends to occur when you’re preoccupied with the person who has what you want, while benign envy is when you focus on what it is that you want. The Right Reverend Allen Shin, Bishop Suffragan of the Episcopal Diocese of New York, recently said that with malicious envy you cede your agency to the person you envy. But when you try to figure out how to get what you want, you keep your agency.

After examining your envy and figuring out the intangible desire, the next step is to figure out some “skill-building microactions.” Ask yourself: “What tiny activities should I test out to see if I can get closer to what I want?” If, for example, you realize that the intangible desire from wanting a promotion is financial security, then quitting your job will likely become a costly error. Instead, boosting your personal finance acumen might be a better option. Or, if you’re realizing that a promotion to you means mentoring others, then perhaps learning how to get reengaged with your alumni association and finding ways to mentor younger alumni might be a way to get more immediate satisfaction.

Finally, when we can direct our envy toward meaningful work, deepening relationships and serving others, we can feel more satisfied with our lives and do some good.

#10449. Samsung bets that you’ll either buy a Galaxy S27 Pro or Ultra next year

Samsung is teeing up to kick off 2027 with an all-new lineup of flagship smartphones, and despite rising prices at your local Best Buy, the brand is still hedging that you’re going to pony up for the most premium model available.

As reported by ETNews, Samsung is currently allotting over 70 percent of its total production capabilities to just the Galaxy S27 Ultra and the new Galaxy S27 “Pro” model expected to launch alongside it. That leaves the plain Galaxy S27 and the larger S27+ on the outside looking in. In comparison to this year’s launch, the Galaxy S26 Ultra made up about 50 percent of this series’ production volume, for a grand total of 18 million units.

Historical performance implies Samsung is probably correct here. While big displays are typically what consumers are drawn to, it does appear that the S27 Pro won’t be all that much smaller than the S27+. Considering the Pro should slot in right around the typical price point as the Plus model, it’s not hard to imagine plenty of would-be S27+ buyers moving to the Pro.

For what it’s worth, Samsung betting big on high-end devices usually pays off. We’re on year two of the Fold series seeing big successes — first with the redesigned Fold 7 in 2025, then with the reshaped Fold 8 this year — and the Galaxy S26 Ultra managed to become the best-selling Android phone in Q2 of this year in a list typically populated by iPhones and cheap Galaxy A-series models. Even with prices constantly on the rise, the people yearn for flagship smartphones. You just have to wonder where that ceiling actually is.

#10446. Build a Hardware Diagnostic Log with Vanilla JavaScript

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A device disconnects halfway through a test. The application reports a timeout, the firmware restarts, and the next attempt succeeds. Where should you start?

For developers working with connected devices, browser interfaces, or hardware prototypes, an application error is often only the final symptom. Replacing code without recording the conditions around a failure can leave you chasing the wrong layer.

This tutorial builds a small browser-based diagnostic log. It records measurements, preserves the test conditions, and exports evidence for another developer to review. You need basic HTML and JavaScript knowledge; no framework or connected instrument is required.

1. Define the question before collecting data Consider a hypothetical development board that disconnects when a peripheral starts. Several explanations remain possible: a firmware exception, a transport problem, or a power supply issue. Start with a testable question: “Does the measured supply voltage change when this peripheral starts?” That question tells you what to record and what to keep constant.

Use a known-good board of the same revision where available. Match the firmware, cable, supply, peripheral, and workload. A comparison loses value when several conditions change together.

Record the observation separately from the explanation:

The hypothesis remains provisional. A reading taken after the device restarts does not establish what happened during the failure.

2. Choose evidence that answers the question Application logs, firmware traces, and bench measurements answer different questions. A timeout establishes that an operation did not finish in time; it does not identify a failed component.

For a view of specialist equipment used in phone-board troubleshooting, DIYFIXTOOL’s overview of Chip-Level Diagnostic Tools discusses thermal imaging, BGA X-ray inspection, and inductance testing. Treat it as a vendor-authored introduction to equipment categories; use instrument documentation and board-specific references when interpreting measurements.

The log below deliberately leaves interpretation to the operator. Enter a numeric value, its unit, and the conditions under which it was measured. Do not turn an isolated reading into an automatic “faulty chip” verdict.

For physical measurements, follow the board and instrument documentation and work within your training. This tutorial covers the software record rather than a procedure for probing or repairing a powered device. 3. Build a small, accessible form

Save the following as index.html and serve it through your usual local development server. For example, if Python is installed, run python -m http. server 8000 in its directory, then open http://localhost:8000. 4. Preserve data without hiding failures

The application stores an array of records as JSON. On reload, it parses that JSON and checks the expected field types before rendering it. Parsing alone does not validate the structure of stored data.

SitePoint’s guide to looping through JSON responses provides useful background on working with objects and arrays after parsing JSON. Each table cell uses textContent, so a note containing HTML is displayed as text rather than inserted as markup. The MDN documentation for textContent explains this behavior.

Storage operations sit inside try...catch blocks because browser persistence can fail. The interface keeps new measurements in memory and offers an export when saving fails. It does not claim those measurements will survive a reload. For another practical vanilla JavaScript project, SitePoint’s **Markdown previewer tutorial **explores browser UI construction and persistence.

As **MDN’s localStorage documentation **explains, storage belongs to the document’s origin. Opening the application on a different port may therefore show a different log. This prototype is a single-browser tool, so export important sessions and avoid recording customer identifiers or private device contents.

5. Compare measurements under matching conditions Suppose two hypothetical readings are 3.29 V and 3.08 V. Their difference is −0.21 V. That arithmetic is straightforward; its meaning depends on the rail specification, measurement uncertainty, workload, and timing.

Do not add a universal voltage threshold to the application. A device-specific limit should come from its specification or an established test procedure.

If the failure is brief, a manually entered steady-state measurement may miss it entirely. Record that limitation. The next investigation may require a time-correlated capture rather than another static reading.

When sharing a session, include the firmware revision, board revision, instrument settings, and reproduction steps. A colleague should be able to repeat the comparison without guessing how the reading was obtained. 6. Verify the workflow before relying on it Try adding a decimal reading and a negative reading, then reload the page. Confirm that both values and their units remain intact. Enter a note containing test and check that it appears literally in the table.

Export the JSON and inspect the record count. Then simulate blocked storage and confirm that the interface reports the failure while allowing an export of the current session.

For a larger application, add editable entries, instrument metadata, and explicit baseline records. A shared service would also need access controls, server-side validation, and a policy for retention. These additions should follow the needs of the diagnostic workflow.

Turn a symptom into a reproducible investigation

The finished prototype captures a useful minimum: what was measured, where, when, and under which conditions. Its value comes from preserving evidence that another person can inspect.

When an application error crosses into firmware or hardware, that record helps you choose the next experiment. Repeat the failure, change one variable, and document what the new evidence supports before deciding what to fix.

#10441. Google Workspace vs. Microsoft 365 vs. Proton Workspace: Which Is Best for Developers and Freelancers?

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Think about what's sitting in your inbox and Drive right now. Client contracts and invoices. Project specs under NDA. Staging credentials a client emailed you. That API key or password you meant to delete.

For most developers and freelancers, all of it lives in Google Workspace or Microsoft 365. Both are excellent tools, and both encrypt your data in transit and at rest. But in their standard setup, the provider holds the encryption keys, which means your provider (and the integrated apps and AI features connected to it) can access what's inside.

Proton Workspace takes a different approach: the same everyday tools, with encryption designed so that not even Proton can read your data.

Here's how the three compare, what each does best, and which makes the most sense for how you work.

Google and Microsoft are built around ecosystem integration. Proton is built around keeping your data yours, without sacrificing productivity tools.

Google Workspace is the go-to suite for startups, agencies and freelancers, and for good reason. Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Calendar and Meet work together seamlessly, and several people can edit the same file in real time without emailing versions back and forth.

Google encrypts data at rest and in transit, and offers client-side encryption on eligible editions. But that extra layer requires higher-tier plans and configuration, so in the default experience Google holds the keys. A password manager and VPN aren't part of the suite.

Best for: Teams whose top priorities are real-time collaboration and third-party integrations.

If your work runs on Word, Excel and Outlook, Microsoft 365 needs little introduction. Business Standard includes full desktop apps, and Excel remains the benchmark for heavy spreadsheet work.

That breadth comes with complexity. Licensing, permissions and device management can eat into time a small team or solo developer would rather spend shipping. And like Google, Microsoft's everyday productivity experience isn't built around end-to-end encryption, while Copilot and advanced security features add cost.

Best for: Businesses built on desktop Office apps and established Microsoft workflows.

Everything is managed from one admin console, with one bill.

This is the core difference. Proton uses zero-access encryption: your data is encrypted before it reaches Proton's servers, and Proton never holds the keys. Proton can't read your data. Not won't. Can't.

The honest trade-offs: Proton Docs and Sheets cover core editing and collaboration, not every advanced Excel feature. There's no presentation app yet, and the third-party integration ecosystem is smaller than Google's or Microsoft's.

The headline prices are close. The real cost isn't:

Proton Workspace covers business email, 1 TB of encrypted storage, docs, sheets, video calls, a password manager and a VPN. That's one bill instead of three.

Need more? Workspace Premium and adds 3 TB of storage per user, 20 custom domains, meetings for up to 250 participants, Lumo private AI and email data retention policies for only $7 more per month. Both plans include a 14-day free trial, and annual plans are currently up to 20% off.

Choose Google Workspace if your team lives in real-time collaboration and relies heavily on Google's integration ecosystem.

Choose Microsoft 365 if your work depends on desktop Excel, PowerPoint and established Microsoft workflows.

Less than you might expect. Proton's Easy Switch tool imports email, contacts and calendars from Google Workspace and other providers, and you keep your custom domain, so clients won't notice a thing. Smaller teams can migrate on their own, and Proton's business team supports larger moves.

Moving from Microsoft 365? Check the migration options for each data type rather than assuming every workflow transfers automatically.

Is Proton Workspace a good alternative to Google Workspace for developers?

Can Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 read my email and files?

By default, yes. Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 hold the encryption keys, and their default terms give them access to your data.

No. Zero-access encryption means Proton never holds the keys to your stored data. Emails between Proton users are end-to-end encrypted automatically, and you can send password-protected encrypted emails to anyone.

Yes. Proton's apps are open source and independently audited.

Yes. Proton Mail Bridge connects Outlook, Apple Mail and Thunderbird.

Does Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 use my data to train AI?

It can. If your plan allows Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 to hold the encryption keys, they can access your data and use it to train their integrated AI models.

No. Proton can't read your data, so it can't use it for AI training.

Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 are mature, capable platforms, and if your work depends on advanced Excel or a deep web of Google integrations, there's a good case for using them.

But if you're a freelancer or a developer or running a small team, Proton Workspace is the stronger choice. You get the same core tools for less money, a password manager and VPN you'd otherwise pay for separately, and encryption that keeps client data, code and credentials readable only by you.

#10440. Hunter is killing Google Home, Alexa controls for its smart ceiling fans

Hunter, a major brand for ceiling fans in the US, is pulling the plug on its Google Home and Amazon Alexa bridge for controlling “HunterSMART” models in just a few weeks.

Effective January 1, 2027, Hunter will pull support for the cloud-reliant “HunterSMART” connection used for Google Home and Amazon Alexa controls. Hunter’s app and the included remote will continue to work, but connections to smart home ecosystems will not.

Beginning January 1, 2027, the legacy cloud-to-cloud connections used for app linking between the HunterSMART™ mobile apps and Google Home and/or Amazon Alexa will no longer be supported.

After this date, Google home and Alexa functionality that relies on this legacy cloud connection will no longer work for HunterSMART fans, including voice commands, scenes, and automations.

This bridge is going away in favor of a Matter connection, with Hunter having been upgrading select models to be Matter-compatible over the past year. But this is only available to “eligible” models, not everyone who was already using Hunter’s existing bridge. A list of compatible models is available on Hunter’s website, with firmware updates rolling out via the HunterSMART app.

Some models, such as the one I reviewed a few years ago, require updated hardware. Besides that, the one I have can’t even be re-connected to Wi-Fi to check for an update as Hunter’s Android app consistently crashes during the setup process.

Once the fan has been updated, it won’t be available via the existing link and will instead require re-pairing via your smart home app of choice, whether that’s Google Home or another.

…Hunter is transitioning eligible HunterSMART™ products to Matter, an industry standard designed to support broader smart-home compatibility.

If your fan is eligible for Matter-compatibility, you will be able to continue using all smart functionality within the Google Home and/or Alexa ecosystems after completing the applicable Matter migration & setup.

Once your HunterSMART fan is Matter-enabled, connecting your fan to Google and Alexa will work differently than it does today. Instead of linking your HunterSMART account to Google Home or Alexa, you will need to setup your Matter-enabled fan directly into these compatible ecosystems using the Matter setup available via the Google Home and/or Alexa apps. Matter-enabled devices do not use the legacy cloud linking service for smart controls that is being discontinued.

How can I migrate my HunterSMART fan to Matter?

Depending on your fan model and hardware configuration, a firmware update or updated hardware components may be required for Matter compatibility. Available Matter upgrade options and instructions will vary by product. You can visit our HunterSMART™ Matter resource page for the latest information about Matter compatibility, available upgrade options, and next steps.

Nvidia's Board of Directors is preparing to oust co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang following revelations of two extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of working for Chinese intelligence and another with an Nvidia executive, reports The Wall Street Journal. Although no final decision has been made yet, the company's directors could meet as early as November 11 to discuss Huang's future. Whoever succeeds Huang will be the company's second CEO in 33 years. Nvidia's stock dropped 8% in after-hours trading following the reports. Nvidia's board of directors launched an independent investigation into the matter on November 8.

The report from the WSJ comes hours after the New York Times revealed that Huang allegedly had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reports directly to him. According to five people who worked at Nvidia, the relationship was known internally, while Huang and Powell were reportedly seen together at a San Jose hotel during Nvidia's GTC conference in March. The allegations follow an earlier report that Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese intelligence asset.

A similar controversy cost Intel chief executive Brian Krzanich his position in June 2018, when an internal investigation confirmed that he had maintained a consensual relationship with an employee, which violated the company's non-fraternization policy applicable to all managers. It is noteworthy that Nvidia's code of conduct explicitly identifies personal relationships as potential conflicts of interest and instructs employees to consult the company's legal department when such conflicts arise. Whether Huang violated Nvidia's internal policies remains unclear, as the code of conduct does not explicitly prohibit all relationships between managers and subordinates.

Huang's potential departure would mark the first CEO transition in Nvidia's 33-year history, and therefore his succession has become an immediate concern for Nvidia, which does not have anyone of Huang's caliber in the leadership team. Although chief financial officer Colette Kress could potentially serve as interim chief executive if Huang is ousted while the BoD searches for a permanent replacement, it remains to be seen how Wall Street would react to this assignment.

Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky, who used to be the company's senior vice president of engineering and operations and remains a member of the company's board and an Nvidia Fellow, could also play a role in the succession process, given his extensive knowledge of Nvidia's technology, corporate culture, and history. However, has not served in an executive role at Nvidia for at least a decade, so the chances that he will succeed Huang are low.

Back on Sunday, directors expressed confidence in Jensen Huang and his leadership team, a choice of words that did not exactly guarantee his continued tenure.

#10437. Googlebook apps built by Googlers add macOS-like status bar shortcuts, keyboard commands

Googlebooks are a bit starved of desktop-class features at launch, but one of Google’s pitches around this platform is how apps can be built for it, and the company’s own employees are showing off what that looks like with some clever apps that just so happen to add features that feel a lot like they’re replicating macOS staples.

In a Reddit thread, three Googlebook apps built by Googlers through Antigravity are shown off, and they’re pretty cool, regardless of how you might feel about the platform itself.

“BentoBox” is a utility that gives you control over the status bar on Googlebook, enabling you to fill the status bar with shortcuts, mini-apps, and more. It’s full of glancable information such as weather conditions, battery charging speeds, and more, but also includes useful tools such as being able to access a clipboard history, set a timer, and more. The app requires permissions including accessibility overlays, but it works like a charm.

I had no idea the status bar on Googlebook could even be used like this, and it really makes that space a lot more useful. Of course, you have to draw a comparison here to macOS, which also uses this space for app shortcuts and tools, though BentoBox offers a different type of customization.

BentoBox is available for download via Google Play for free.

The other Mac-like app here is “Booklight,” a launcher that’s basically Apple’s Spotlight, just for Googlebook. It has a transparent design and lets you search “apps, settings, and the web.”

Technically, Googlebook already can do this in its built-in search bar (in the app drawer), but Booklight has more customization and functionality, including being able to write out shorthand commands all in one sentence with the app then completing the command in the appropriate apps, as well as having a clearer UI for experiences such as typing in quick math equations. It’s also good at finding symbols (so you don’t have to remember the U+ codes that carried over from ChromeOS). Not one I found myself wanting to use, but the potential is there.

Both BentoBox and Booklight were developed by Alexander Kuscher, VP over Laptops & Tablets at Google.

The other app highlighted in Google’s thread was Wayfinder, a file manager app described as a “desktop-grade file manager.” The big bonus here is network file access for NAS boxes and other uses, but the app also just has a more advanced UX compared to Googlebook’s built-in Files app.

Googlebook’s app gap is a real problem at launch, but these apps do show there’s a lot of potential in the platform, it’s just a matter of getting developers on board – which itself will require Google and its partners to actually sell some of these laptops… classic chicken-and-egg situation.

The hub now tells the console it’s Nintendo’s own dock.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A hobbyist going by mkopec turned an approximately $45 Cable Matters USB-C hub into a working Nintendo Switch 2 dock, using only about 540 bytes of code to mod the firmware. That mod lets the hub masquerade as an official dock, as mkopec detailed in a blog post. The edited firmware replies to Nintendo’s vendor messages and returns the same identity as the official dock, and makes TV mode work, which was not the case with the hub’s stock firmware. A separate fix with minor firmware rewriting also corrects washed-out HDR over HDMI, a nice bonus.

The modder, who writes that “Nintendo went in a proprietary direction (as they so often do),” decided to modify the hub’s firmware to make a working travel dock, as Nintendo’s official dock can be bulky. Unlocking the additional functionality did not come with a noticeable cost, as the hub “still works normally with my PC and my phone.” Grabbing an off-the-shelf USB-C hub and turning it into something more is quite the trick.

The stock hub has no problem charging the console, but it shows no picture, even though it negotiates both power and DisplayPort Alt Mode. Capturing the official Switch 2 dock’s traffic with a USB Power Delivery (USB-PD) sniffer, the modder found that it advertises two Standard or Vendor IDs: one for DisplayPort and one for Nintendo’s own mode.

The console enters Nintendo’s mode first, then DisplayPort, and, once DisplayPort is configured, it sends Nintendo’s vendor messages. This is the exchange of proprietary messages for negotiation, although the company told us last year that it “does not have any intention to hinder or invalidate legal third-party dock compatibility.”

The modification only required adding about 540 bytes to a firmware of just 32 KiB. The Cable Matters 7-in-1 triple display hub, like most, is simply an amalgamation of separate, specialized chips, in this case: a VL103 as the USB-PD controller, a VL817 USB hub chip for the USB ports, an RTD2142 DisplayPort Multi-Stream Transport chip for the DisplayPort-to-HDMI function, and XT25F16B flash memory chips. The VL chips are from VIA Labs, the RTD2142 is from Realtek, and the stock hub reports VIA’s vendor ID, which is an identity that needed to be changed for this mod.

The modder first used the WITRN K2 inline USB-PD sniffer on the official dock. Then, it was a matter of dumping the VL103’s firmware with the vli plugin of fwupd, the Linux firmware update tool, before flashing the VL103 with the changes over USB and through the VL817.

Changes were made incrementally, with seven versions in all, starting with answers to Nintendo’s discovery, mode entry, and echo commands, then an update to power delivery to offer 15 V at 2.8 A like the dock, changing the reported vendor ID to Nintendo’s, masquerading entirely as the official dock and getting TV mode working, and finally a full sequence match that removed a pause of about 3 seconds.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The process appears to contradict claims two accessory makers made to The Verge that the dock check uses encryption with a dedicated chip, as, in this case, copied identity data and fixed replies were sufficient.

Getting TV mode to work would have already been an accomplishment worth celebrating, but the modder took it further: the picture over HDMI was washed out with HDR turned on, and it was simply a matter of narrowing down the cause. The end theory was a mistake in how the hub’s AVI InfoFrame signaled BT.709, the standard dynamic range color space, instead of HDR’s wider BT.2020.

The theory was confirmed by a 108-byte patch to the RTD2142’s firmware, flashed with flashrom over I2C carried on the DisplayPort AUX channel through the same USB-C cable, which marks the signal as BT.2020 whenever HDR is in use. One third-party dock’s firmware contains a debug string, “switch2 color space patch,” which suggests this is a known issue. HDR through the hub’s own DisplayPort port is still washed out.

Separately, the hub’s firmware has no variable refresh rate (VRR) support, but because the patched hub identifies as the official dock, the console now offers VRR. However, turning VRR on froze the DisplayPort picture, and HDMI remained at 60 Hz. In a separate Linux test, with the hub patched to advertise Adaptive-Sync and an EDID override in place, the screen went black as soon as the frame rate varied, so the feature was left off.

The modder’s post shares no code, patch files, or repository, although the method is well-explained. The USB ports and Ethernet weren't tested rigorously, and the post does not say which Switch 2 system version was used. The modder also doesn’t understand many of Nintendo’s commands, so the hub’s version replies are copies of the official dock’s, and unrecognized commands still get the hub’s stock reply.

That’s important because Nintendo’s system update 21.0.0 left some third-party docks charging but with no video output. While vendors provided updated firmware as a fix, the modder’s ad hoc solution has no vendor behind it, so would-be modders could end up on their own.

Google announced today that Fitbit Sense and Versa smartwatches will soon lose the ability to “install or update third-party apps and clocks.”

This change to the Fitbit App Gallery applies to the Versa, Versa 2, Versa 3, Versa 4, Sense, and Sense 2.

Existing “third-party apps or clock faces installed on your Fitbit device” will remain available, but you can no longer download new ones (or update them) starting November 28. The November 28 deadline also applies to third-party developers. Google will “no longer support uploading new apps and clock faces or updating existing ones.”

Google winding down Fitbit OS for smartwatches is not particularly surprising as the company has been all-in on Wear OS and the Pixel Watch. That said, the Sense 2 and Versa 4 should probably no longer be on sale.

#10432. Prompt Management in TypeScript: LangSmith vs Git vs 3 Open-Source Registries

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every prompt registry we tested can change a prompt in a running TypeScript app, roll it back, and give production and staging different versions. LangSmith's prompt hub, Langfuse, Phoenix and AcruxCore all passed those three tests. The real differences show up elsewhere: which template syntax each one accepts, how many npm packages it pulls in, how long a change takes to reach the app, and what happens when the registry is down.

We tested all of this with one small app and one prompt, which has a condition and a loop. Git files served as the baseline. Every number below comes from a recorded run.

Most teams start with prompts in code: a template string, or a .txt file next to the code that uses it. That works until a product manager wants to change one sentence, and the change has to wait for a full release.

A prompt registry moves the text out of the deploy. The app fetches the prompt by name and by a label such as production. You change which version the label points to, and the app picks up the new text without a deploy.

LangSmith's prompt hub is the best-known registry, but it is not the only one. Several of the LangSmith alternatives also manage prompts, and three of them are open source and self-hostable: Langfuse, Phoenix and AcruxCore. We covered how those tools handle tracing in Self-Hosted LangSmith Alternatives: 4 Tools Tested on One TypeScript Agent. This article covers prompts only.

Every tool got the same prompt, support-reply. Its template takes three variables: a customer name, a plan, and a list of help articles. It has one condition: a priority line appears only for premium customers. It also has one loop: one line per help article. In Jinja2 syntax, the template looks like this:

One help article contains the text Settings > Export. We included it on purpose, to catch any tool that HTML-escapes > into >.

Every tool then ran the same sequence from a TypeScript script:

Each tool used its own documented TypeScript SDK. The four registries passed all six steps. The rest of this article covers how each one got there, and what it cost.

Keeping prompts in the repository costs almost nothing. The template sits in prompts/support-reply.njk, and nunjucks, the JavaScript port of Jinja2, renders it:

The autoescape: false line matters. Our first version called nunjucks.renderString() directly, and the test failed. The default environment HTML-escapes its output, so Settings > Export reached the model as Settings > Export. Escaping is correct for web pages and wrong for prompts.

Git gives you full Jinja2, code review on every prompt change, and history in the same place as the code. What it can't do is change a prompt in a running app. Every edit, and every rollback, waits for a deploy.

LangSmith stores a prompt as a serialized LangChain object (ChatPromptTemplate), not as plain text. LangSmith's own documentation says you must use the LangChain npm package to pull prompts in TypeScript (Manage prompts programmatically). So a plain TypeScript app that uses the openai package still needs langchain and @langchain/core:

Those three packages installed 23 packages and 70 MB. Most of the size is @langchain/* (27 MB) and js-tiktoken (22 MB).

Templates. In TypeScript, LangChain accepts f-string and mustache templates. Mustache sections ({{#docs}}…{{/docs}}) handled our loop. Mustache has no ==, though, so the premium check became an is_premium boolean computed in code. We also tried templateFormat: "jinja2", which LangChain's Python package supports. In TypeScript it threw DEFAULT_PARSER_MAPPING[templateFormat] is not a function.

Labels and rollback. production and staging are reserved tags, and the documentation moves them in the UI. The langsmith JavaScript client has no public method that moves a tag. Our script called the same REST route the SDK uses internally (POST /api/v1/repos/-//tags). It worked, but it is not a documented API.

Caching. The SDK caches prompts for 300 seconds by default. In our test, a running app saw the new version 300 seconds after we moved the tag.

Langfuse's TypeScript client is one package, @langfuse/client. It installed 5 packages and 8 MB:

Creating a version, moving a label and reading by label are all public SDK calls: prompt.create, prompt.update and prompt.get (Get started with prompt management).

Templates. The documentation shows only {{variable}} substitution. But compile() calls the mustache library, so sections worked for our loop. The type signature accepts only string values, so passing a list needed a cast. The Langfuse UI colours the section tags red, and it lists title and body as the prompt's variables, not docs or is_premium. We would not depend on behaviour the documentation doesn't promise. When we sent the Jinja2 version instead, Langfuse returned the {% if %} and {% for %} tags unchanged, with no error. The model would have received them as text.

Caching. The cache time is 60 seconds by default (Caching). Our app saw the change after 62 seconds. Langfuse is also the only client with a fallback option: a prompt string the SDK uses when it cannot reach the server on a cold start.

Phoenix's TypeScript client fetches a prompt by name and tag, and toSDK() converts it into the message format the openai package expects. Phoenix templates only replace variables, so the condition and the loop have to run in your code before rendering:

That is 16 lines, against 6 to 8 for the other registries. All the extra lines are template logic that now lives in the app.

Templates. Phoenix offers MUSTACHE, F_STRING and NONE formats (Prompts reference). Even in MUSTACHE mode, though, rendering is a plain replacement of {{name}}. When we sent mustache sections, they came back unchanged, with no error.

Errors. getPrompt() catches every error, logs it and returns null. You can see this in the client source, src/utils/getPromptBySelector.ts. A missing prompt and an unreachable server look the same to your code, which is why the snippet checks for null.

Size and caching. The client installed 57 packages and 90 MB. Most of that is OpenTelemetry, which comes in through its @arizeai/phoenix-otel dependency. The client has no prompt cache, so every render is a network call. That is also why a label change showed up immediately: 0 seconds in our test.

AcruxCore stores Jinja2 templates and renders them on the server with nunjucks. The SDK sends the variables and gets back finished messages:

The template from the test section works as it is, condition and loop included, with no is_premium flag computed in code. A label is called an alias here, and promoteAlias() moves it (Manage prompts via the SDK). The SDK installed 3 packages and 12 MB. Most of the 12 MB is one OpenTelemetry package, @opentelemetry/semantic-conventions.

Templates. Jinja2 only. When we committed the mustache version, AcruxCore rejected it at commit time with Template parse error: unexpected token: #. That is a clear error, but it also means that moving mustache prompts from LangSmith or Langfuse requires rewriting them.

We sent the same two templates, a Jinja2 one and a mustache one, to each tool's own renderer:

The rows that matter most are the ones where the tags were left in the output, because those failures produce no error. The model receives raw template syntax, and the only symptom is a strange answer. Whatever tool you pick, test one prompt with logic in it before you move the rest.

Putting logic in the template is not automatically better. It lets someone change the condition without a deploy. It also lets them break the condition without a deploy. Keeping logic in code, as Phoenix forces you to do, puts every branch under code review and in your tests.

A registry is a new runtime dependency, so we tested an outage. The app reached each registry through a local proxy, and we switched the proxy off. A separate process then started while the registry was still unreachable.

LangSmith, Langfuse and AcruxCore keep serving the last good version while the registry is down, even after the cache time has passed. The risk is a cold start: a new container or a serverless function that boots during the outage. Langfuse's fallback option is the built-in answer to that. With the other tools, keep a copy of each prompt in your code as a fallback, which brings back part of the Git setup.

Keep prompts in Git if engineers make every prompt change and your deploys are quick. Set autoescape: false, and you get Jinja2, reviews and history for free.

Use LangSmith's prompt hub if you already use LangChain, or already trace with LangSmith. If your app doesn't use LangChain, budget for the extra dependency and for the tag moves that only the UI supports.

Use Langfuse if you want a small client, a local compile(), and a fallback for cold starts. Keep to {{variable}} substitution unless you are comfortable relying on mustache behaviour that the documentation doesn't promise.

Use Phoenix if you already use it for tracing, or if you prefer all template logic in code. Remember the null check, and that every render is a network call.

Use AcruxCore if you want real conditions and loops in the template and rendering on the server. Expect one network call per new set of variables, and a personal API key for writes.

Before you choose, run one of your own prompts with real logic in it through the tool's SDK, not through its playground. Two of the four registries we tested failed on template syntax without any error, and an SDK run is where you would see that.

The AI data center boom is bringing hope to struggling cannabis farmers as they face increased competition, costs, and taxes amid reduced demand for marijuana. According to Arizona Public Media, the cannabis industry is in decline, with sales peaking in 2024 and oversupply driving prices down. And now, several growers are considering selling their cultivation facilities or converting them into “mini data center nodes.” These facilities already have many of the ingredients needed for AI data centers, such as the increasingly hard-to-get supply of electricity and water infrastructure.

"For some reason, there's a lot more cannabis grown in Arizona than Arizonans use. And so, a lot of folks are getting out of that business, like myself, at least on the cultivation side. But these facilities can potentially be repurposed to be mini data center nodes," Moe Asnani, the former owner of two Tucson D2 Dispensaries, told the public broadcaster. He also added, "The whole idea is if you create these smaller nodes where people control their own data, where they're not at the mercy of other people's updates and things like that — that's kind of where the idea came in, because I believe in decentralization."

Cannabis farming is both power- and water-intensive. Forbes looked at a 32,850-square-foot cannabis facility in Kalamazoo, Michigan, which is currently wired for 1.5 megawatts, which can be expanded to 2.5 megawatts in under a year and 15 megawatts in the long term. It's also provisioned for fiber internet and equipped with a state-of-the-art HVAC system for climate control, which should make it a tempting property for anyone wanting to put up a small data center — something that even OpenAI and Anthropic are interested in as massive hyperscale sites face opposition from the community.

This concept is dubbed "adaptive reuse," with Tucson City Council member Paul Cunningham saying that it’s a more palatable alternative to massive, purpose-built sites sitting on the outskirts of town. "Data centers are dirty words, and everybody knows that. And no one wants to build a brand-new data center anywhere," the politician said. "But if we have buildings that were using that amount of water and that amount of energy already in their previous function and [it] can be done without being invasive, I'm OK with exploring that option."

There is massive demand for data centers, but it’s not a guaranteed payoff for struggling cash-strapped growers looking to unload their unprofitable properties. Niki Krear, vice president of acquisitions of real estate investment trust New Lake Capital Partners, said that there’s a sweet spot between connectivity, costs, and regulation that data center operators look for in a site.

"It’s a combination of finding affordable power, dense fiber networks, and favorable tax policies," Krear told MJBizDaily. Even though many cultivation facilities already boast higher-than-average power capacity for lighting and climate control, data centers often demand twice to thrice more, with upgrades possibly taking up to five years.

Data center operators looking for smaller sites may also have to contend with NIMBY — not in my backyard — fights from neighbors. Additionally, there may be zoning restrictions, moratoriums, and regulatory hurdles, and the lack of economies of scale could end up costing operators more.

This is particularly important as AI chips are expected to increase in power and efficiency in the next five years. As these new AI GPUs become available, data centers will need to sell their existing equipment and buy new hardware to remain competitive. Because suppliers usually offer favorable pricing for larger orders, upgrading these smaller sites will likely end up being more expensive on a per-unit basis. That said, growing opposition toward large new projects could make these former cannabis farms suitable alternatives for operators desperate to get more compute online quickly, provided they check all (or most of) the boxes they need.

New leaks reveal the camera specs for Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy S27 series which includes three lenses across the lineup, but not the upgrades you want, nor what Ultra owners might expect.

SammyGuru reports that Samsung is “evaluating” camera setups for the Galaxy S27, S27+, S27 Pro, and S27 Ultra, and it looks like a mixed bag across the board.

The base Galaxy S27 and S27+ are looking very familiar, with identical main camera sensors to last year, and the same ultrawide sensor that’s been in use since the Galaxy S23 series. The telephoto and selfie sensors are looking at new hardware, but without any major spec upgrades.

Galaxy S27 Pro and Ultra, meanwhile, have a new 200MP main camera on deck, a 50MP ultrawide shooter, and a mere 12MP telephoto. The Ultra might get 5x compared to the Pro’s 3x optical zoom, but with a secondary telephoto lens going missing, existing users of the lineup are sure to be disappointed.

Notably, SammyGuru’s article mentions the Pro as using “the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s 3x sensor,” but shows the 12MP Samsung S5K3LD in that place instead. As RAMageddon rages on and Samsung hunts for new ways to balance specs vs price, cameras are a place that’s obviously going to be cut, but competitors are already running laps around Samsung on the hardware front. AI-generated videos are becoming an important part of modern web design. Designers can now create animated backgrounds, product demonstrations, hero section videos, and visual storytelling elements without relying entirely on traditional video production. However, generating a visually appealing video is only one part of the process. To use AI-generated videos effectively on a website, developers and designers must also understand video formats, visual quality, file optimization, and website performance.

These technical factors directly influence how videos appear across devices, how quickly pages load, and how smoothly visitors interact with a website.

Video format selection is one of the first technical decisions when preparing AI-generated assets for the web. Different formats offer different levels of compression, compatibility, and visual quality.

For most websites, MP4 with H.264 remains a dependable default. WebM or AV1 can be offered as additional formats where appropriate.

Developers should also consider browser compatibility before selecting a format. Providing multiple sources allows browsers to choose a supported option.

AI-generated videos can sometimes contain visual inconsistencies, unnatural movements, distorted objects, or changes in lighting between frames. These issues become more noticeable when videos are displayed in large website sections.

Resolution is an important factor in maintaining visual quality. Common resolutions include:

However, higher resolution does not automatically mean better website performance or user experience. A 4K video may look impressive, but loading it unnecessarily can increase bandwidth consumption.

Frame rate also affects the viewing experience. Many website videos work well at 24 or 30 frames per second. Higher frame rates may be useful for fast-moving scenes, but they also increase the amount of visual data that needs to be processed.

Designers should review AI-generated footage before publishing it. Checking transitions, motion consistency, sharpness, and color accuracy helps prevent distracting visual problems.

Large video files can significantly increase website loading times. This is especially important for websites with video backgrounds, animated landing pages, and multiple visual sections.

Video optimization involves reducing file size without making the footage noticeably worse.

Some practical optimization techniques include:

Compression: Video compression reduces unnecessary data while preserving important visual details. Developers can use encoding tools such as FFmpeg to adjust bitrate, resolution, and codec settings.

Bitrate control: Bitrate determines how much data is used to represent each second of video. A higher bitrate generally preserves more detail but increases file size. Selecting an appropriate bitrate depends on the video's resolution, movement, and intended display size.

Trimming unnecessary footage: Website videos rarely need to be several minutes long. Removing unused sections helps reduce file size and keeps visual content focused.

Removing unnecessary audio: Background videos that do not require sound should be exported without an audio track. This reduces unnecessary data and supports a cleaner user experience.

Responsive video delivery: Websites should serve appropriately sized assets for different screen sizes. A smaller video may be sufficient for mobile users, while desktop visitors can receive a higher-resolution version.

These techniques help developers balance visual quality with efficient content delivery.

Even a well-optimized video can affect website performance if it is implemented incorrectly. Developers should consider how videos are loaded, displayed, and processed by browsers.

For example, automatically loading several large videos when a page opens can consume significant bandwidth. Instead, developers can use lazy loading strategies for videos that appear further down the page.

For background videos, the HTML video element offers several useful attributes:

Developers should also avoid autoplaying large videos unnecessarily. A static image can often provide a better experience on mobile devices or slower connections.

Performance testing tools such as Google Lighthouse and Chrome DevTools can help identify whether video assets are affecting loading speed, bandwidth usage, or rendering performance.

Technical optimization should not come at the expense of accessibility. Background videos should not distract users or make website content difficult to understand.

Developers should respect the prefers-reduced-motion media query, which allows users who prefer reduced animation to receive a less motion-intensive experience.

A suitable static background image can be displayed as an alternative.

Mobile compatibility is equally important. Smaller screens, limited data plans, and varying network conditions can make heavy video assets less practical. Testing videos on different devices and connection speeds helps identify potential problems before publication.

AI-generated video assets offer exciting possibilities for modern web design, but their successful implementation requires more than creative output. Choosing suitable video formats, maintaining consistent visual quality, compressing files, and considering website performance are all essential parts of the development process.

By combining thoughtful video production with responsive delivery, accessibility considerations, and performance testing, designers and developers can create engaging websites without compromising loading speed or usability. As AI video technology continues to evolve, understanding these technical fundamentals will remain valuable for building efficient and visually appealing web experiences.

The most dangerous thing in the world is a bored engineer with a screwdriver. If you see a soldering iron, run for the hills.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Enterprising techies looking to build their own local AI cluster have far more interesting options than buying DGX Sparks or Apple Mac Studios. Used data center GPUs are everywhere, and a server rack's garbage is an enthusiast's treasure. This option has become even more popular with CMPunlocker, a soft-mod for Nvidia CMP-170HX cards that unlocks abilities well beyond stock. Now, a techie has taken it a step further, blasting through the remaining limitations with voltage glitching and creating a card faster than the actual $20,000 Nvidia A100 GPU with 80GB of VRAM... but from an $2,500 8GB CMP-170HX mining card.

The volt-mod was done by Kate (GitHub link here), who got her starting point from a paper that described how one could exploit GA100 cards' microcode. She turned her attention to the normally protected onboard fuse controller. Although it's rarely discussed, a "fuse box" has been integral in most any CPU and GPU for a while — though it's normally used once at the factory to break physical connections in chips to parts that have tested poorly, thus disabling them so they can be sold as a lower-end model.

If you're wondering how people are getting 80-40GB of VRAM out of 8-10GB, the explanation is simple: the GA100 silicon actually includes all the corresponding HBM2e VRAM dies within; but they get disabled at the factory like the shader modules. The smaller version is more desirable, as it's based on the variant of GA100 with 80GB of HBM2e within, while the 10GB cards spawn from the 40GB GA100.

The Nvidia cards in question have quite an elaborate eFuse controller (16,384 in a 512 x 32 array) — which can be read to obtain the card's current configuration. Most every part of the card has related fuses: VRAM sections, individual shader modules, PCIe 4.0 and NVLink, and even video codec hardware. However, as Kate succinctly put it: Nvidia's design is insecure, as popping fuses can grant access to more features, not fewer.

Under normal conditions, these fuses can't be popped, or "written to," by the user — but a geek armed with a soldering iron isn't a normal user. Kate had GPT-6 Astra design a simple circuit board based on an $8 STM32G4 microcontroller to tap into the power signals on the card's PCB.

The voltage regulators (VRMs) on the card "speak" PWMVID, an Nvidia standard, and Kate's board intercepted the PWM signals sent into the VRM controller, forcing it to produce voltage glitches on the line feeding the GPU, where the fuse controller lies.

Remember when we said the fuse controller was read-only? With the voltage glitches, many fuse-status reads in a tight loop, and she managed to set the controller to a state in which its security bit flags allowed writes through. From that point, it was "easy" to reconfigure her card. She was careful to force-disable any shader modules previously marked as defective, because these are physical fuses — there's no "undo" button.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

She applied the mod to her cards and, after testing with multiple workloads, found that nine had the full 80 GB of VRAM working, and one card "only" had 64 GB usable. Most interestingly, unlocking all the shader modules (SM) nets her FP16 FMA performance 20% beyond a regular A100 card. She thinks this is due to the chips often having 120 or more usable SMs — over the 108 on the spec sheet. The GA100 die starts with 128 SMs to account for defects, which is normal in chip manufacturing.

The CMPUnlocker soft mod is required for enabling the "new" features on the drivers, but it doesn't unlock the card's full potential: the VRAM upper limit is 40-64GB (depending on the variant), many shader modules remain locked, and PCIe bandwidth only goes to 2.0. Additionally, there's no ECC, NVLink, or multi-instance GPU support, all of which are critical in a server setup and are also used for product segmentation.

Kate's volt-mod does away with all of these limits, and her best test card is happily working at PCIe 4.0 speed with the full feature set. She didn't test the video encoder bits, but it's unlikely anybody using these cards cares much for that.

As for the cost, a CMP-170HX 8GB is currently hovering around $3,000, and the 10GB variant costs around $2,500. A full-fat Nvidia A100 80GB in a PCIe configuration can reach $20,000 or more. The SXM server-module versions are cheaper, but they require infrastructure around them. Note that these prices will likely vary significantly, especially as people become increasingly aware of the mods.

Kate says she's publishing her research now because another person independently found the same issue. She has informed Nvidia of the vulnerability, though there's not much the company can do for existing cards already on the market.

#10419. Google reworks TPU silicon into specialized systems for agents and security

Google has yet to share specs, prices or ship dates for either new system.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Google's eighth-generation TPU family has now expanded further. Back in April, the company announced TPU 8t for training AI models and TPU 8i for general-purpose inference workloads. Google has now introduced TPU 8tx, built on the same silicon as the previously announced 8t, for confidential, hardware-isolated inference aimed at regulated enterprises and governments, and TPU 8i Max, which combines two 8i chips on one package for long-context agentic work.

TPU 8tx swaps the Arm-based Axion hosts of the 8t and 8i for a 5th Gen AMD EPYC CPU, adopting a Boardfly network, and the 8i Max doubles the compute, SRAM, and HBM bandwidth of the original 8i. The original split, the TPU 8t and 8i, made natural sense. The 8t targets large-scale training, while the 8i leans toward low-latency inference and reasoning. TPUs have become a fast-growing business, with the company claiming nearly 100 customers, including Meta’s recent move to TPUs. The more modular approach is flexible and can deliver specialized systems “in a matter of months rather than years,” helping that popularity along.

Secure, confidential inference; small-scale training

For the new parts, the TPU 8i Max isn't innovative on the surface, as it’s just two TPU 8i chips combined into a single package. The result is twice the theoretical compute, but more importantly, it fits twice the silicon within the “existing rack footprint,” and Google claims more compute per square foot and per watt.

Doubling both SRAM and HBM bandwidth helps keep things scaling, which would put the 8i Max at about 20.2 FP4 PFLOPS, 768 MB SRAM, and about 17.2 TB/s HBM bandwidth. This compares to Nvidia’s Rubin R200 GPU at a rated 50 FP4 PFLOPS for inference and 22 TB/s of HBM4 per socket, or AMD’s MI455X with 40 FP4 PFLOPS. The compute gap is closing.

The memory bandwidth doubling is also potentially one way around moving to HBM4. The memory wall, as Google calls it, or the bandwidth bottleneck, is a real concern “when dozens of AI agents work together across an entire software codebase.” Larger context windows — with larger models targeting 1 million tokens — mean larger KV caches, partly held in SRAM, and each new token has to read that cache back from memory, which is where the extra HBM bandwidth helps. It’s a different route from Nvidia’s LPX: more bandwidth in one package, rather than a second chip type for decoding and a storage tier for context.

Google also provides useful software for agents to get the most out of its hardware. TPU Sync is an open-source “model-state layer for TPU clusters” that moves KV caches off the chip’s HBM, “automatically tiering massive KV caches off the chip in milliseconds” down to host DRAM and, experimentally, shared storage. Google says this can cut KV transfer latency by “more than 90%,” with time-to-first-token gains that vary by workload. The company has also announced the Agent Compute Engine, a Google Cloud service that pauses idle agent sessions and moves their working memory aside until they’re needed again, another memory-saving effort.

Google credits its vLLM-TorchTPU stack with “state-of-the-art price-performance marks” on InferenceX and AgentX, which test realistic agentic coding and long-context work. However, the only published third-party numbers so far are for the last-generation Ironwood TPU. In SemiAnalysis’s InferenceX tests in September, running Qwen3.5 397B in FP8, Ironwood delivered 50.4% more tokens per dollar than Nvidia’s B200 and 96.0% more than the B300 at 20 tokens per second per user. One issue with that, however, is that Ironwood lacks native FP4, although newer November results show its FP8 beating Nvidia’s FP4 GB300 NVL72 on the same model, at 1.67 times the performance per dollar. There is also no eighth-gen result yet to compare how the new generation differs.

In contrast to the 8i Max, which is designed for long-context work, the new TPU 8tx, “built on the same silicon as TPU 8t,” is “optimized for secure and confidential inference” as well as small-scale training. The security is built into the hardware with isolation to prevent snooping on sensitive data, including model weights. Normally, data has to be unlocked in memory during processing, which is the step this isolation is meant to cover.

This chip is intended for areas where security and confidentiality are high priorities, which means regulated enterprises and governments, particularly those who are using frontier or proprietary models. In that case, the operators may want to “fine-tune models using their private data, distill large models into smaller ones, and train their agents,” without having to move sensitive data between clusters. Agents and security meet here for “secure agent execution.” Back in April, the Pentagon and Google reportedly held discussions for TPU usage in classified settings, although the 8tx chip is not specifically named.

Google’s Private AI Compute, its “hardened TPU platform” with protections “comparable to a typical TEE,” per its September technical brief, already runs confidential serving on TPUs. The 8tx appears to be that capability turned into a product for customers. Alternatives include Nvidia’s NVL72, with one security domain across 72 Rubin GPUs, 36 Vera CPUs, and the interconnects, and Intel’s TDX, which is adding trusted I/O to cover data moving to accelerators.

The TPU 8tx hosts are based on 5th Gen AMD EPYC boards, instead of the Axion hosts on the 8t, which replaced x86 in April. There's one Axion for every two TPUs on the 8i, compared with one Xeon per four on Ironwood. Google gives no reason for the change, but its Confidential VM configuration list has both AMD and Intel series chips, with no Arm-based ones listed. Private AI Compute uses “an AMD-based hardware Trusted Execution Environment” for its CPU workloads, suggesting Google swapped something it already runs on its confidential stack.

The 8tx also adopts the 8i’s Boardfly network over the 8t’s torus, which Google claims can deliver “up to 2x lower latency compared to TPU 8t” with almost no performance penalty, although it’s not clear what measure Google is using. The alternative torus network suits training, since chips mostly swap data with neighbors in a predictable manner, but inference on large mixture-of-experts and reasoning models can send smaller messages between distant chips, with every hop adding delay. With Boardfly, it’s at most seven hops against 16 at 1,024 chips.

What is lacking is a full specifications table, the amount of HBM capacity, pod sizes, an availability date, pricing, and customers for either system. Details on attestation, that is, the ability for the customer to verify confidentiality, are also missing for 8tx. The 8tx and 8i Max are currently listed, along with the 8i and 8t, as “coming soon” on Google’s Cloud TPU page.

Delivering two new TPU systems nearly seven months after April’s pair shows Google wants to turn out specialized systems much more quickly than has been the case in the past. Now, it just needs to prove them, through benchmarks and an availability date when the hardware is actually in customers’ hands.
